analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deductions for employer anti-union campaigns and requires public reporting of that spending.
analysis.headline: 136 House Democrats — and no Republicans — backed the bill, which has sat in the Ways and Means Committee since April 2025 with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax law, companies can write off the money they spend persuading employees not to unionize as an ordinary business expense — meaning other taxpayers effectively help foot the bill. This bill would end that write-off for employer campaigns aimed at workers' decisions about unions and collective bargaining. It would also require companies and the outside "union avoidance" consultants they hire to report that spending to the IRS, with penalties starting at $10,000 or $1,000 per employee for failing to disclose.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers deciding whether to form or join a union gain the most: employer anti-union campaigns would no longer be subsidized by taxpayers, and the campaigns themselves would become more expensive and visible through public reporting. Unions benefit from a fairer playing field in organizing elections. The federal Treasury also gains revenue from the denied deductions. The bill's findings cite research showing employers were charged with labor law violations in roughly 4 of 10 union elections in 2016-2017 and spend about $340 million a year on outside consultants to sway workers.

how_it_helps.text: Ends the federal tax subsidy for employer efforts to influence workers' decisions about unions: the bill adds employer anti-union spending to the list of expenses (like lobbying) that businesses cannot deduct, so other taxpayers stop helping fund those campaigns.

Forces disclosure: employers must report to the IRS the dates, amounts, and nature of spending meant to influence workers on labor organizations, and outside consultants must file similar reports about work done for their clients — making anti-union campaigns traceable rather than buried in general expenses.

Attaches real money to the rules: employers that fail to report face a penalty of $10,000 or $1,000 per full-time employee (whichever is greater), with up to $100,000 in additional penalties if the failure continues past 90 days.

Spares legitimate activity: the bill carves out ordinary bargaining with a recognized union, communications with shareholders, voluntary union recognition, grievance procedures, and legally required workplace postings, so day-to-day labor relations is not swept in.

The bill's findings cite Economic Policy Institute research that employers were charged with unfair labor practices in about 4 of 10 union elections in 2016-2017 (over 54% in larger units) and spent $340 million a year on outside consultants to sway workers — spending that currently reduces their taxes.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that run anti-union campaigns pay: they lose the deduction for that spending and bear new reporting duties and penalties. Companies with large workforces face the steepest exposure, since the reporting penalty scales at $1,000 per full-time employee. All employers whose meetings or trainings touch on labor organizations take on compliance costs and tax complexity, and the Treasury must write implementing regulations. Any lost deductions translate into somewhat higher taxes for the affected companies.

drawbacks.text: The trigger is broad: any meeting or training where labor organizations are discussed becomes non-deductible, which could sweep in routine HR and compliance training and impose real paperwork burdens on employers of all sizes, not just aggressive anti-union campaigns.

Penalties scale with headcount — the greater of $10,000 or $1,000 per full-time employee — so a large company faces a very large base penalty for a filing mistake, though penalties can be waived for reasonable cause and the continuing-failure penalty is capped at $100,000.

The deduction can be denied based on an NLRB complaint or a settlement offer over an unfair labor practice before the charge is finally adjudicated; a full set-aside of the complaint is excepted, but employers could lose deductions over unproven allegations in the meantime.

Writing the rules will be contentious: the Treasury must issue guidance within 240 days of enactment defining what counts as an attempt to 'influence' employees, and ambiguous rules could invite disputes and litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — removing a taxpayer subsidy from employer campaigns against workers' collective bargaining rights, and making those campaigns publicly traceable — is substantial for the millions of workers who consider organizing each year, and the bill's exceptions protect ordinary bargaining and communications. The honest costs are real but manageable: compliance burdens and steep, headcount-scaled penalties could land on employers broadly, and denying deductions based on an unproven NLRB complaint before final adjudication is rough justice. A cleaner version would tie the disallowance to final adverse findings and soften the per-employee penalty, but as drawn the bill's costs fall mainly on the employers whose conduct it targets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee in April 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Norcross introduced the bill on April 7, 2025, with 136 original cosponsors, all of them Democrats.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law; that is the last action on the record.
As of the end of the provided record, the committee has held no markup and the House has taken no vote, so the bill remains pending with the 119th Congress still in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that spend money opposing union organizing, and the union-avoidance consulting industry, are better off with the bill stalled: the tax deduction for that spending and the current lack of disclosure both remain intact. The 137 Democratic sponsors keep a stated position but no policy change has occurred.

for.name: Rep. Donald Norcross
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 136 cosponsors, all Democrats, on the day of introduction.

for.name: 136 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill one of the larger Democratic sponsorship lists of the Congress but no Republican support.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Republican majority)
against.role: Committee of referral; Chairman Jason Smith (R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and, per the action history, has taken no further action — no hearing or markup has been scheduled.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the bill's 137 sponsors or cosponsors is a Republican, and the Republican-controlled chamber has not taken the bill up.

sides.party_line_note: Support is entirely Democratic — 136 cosponsors plus the sponsor, zero Republicans — and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee has not acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Union-avoidance consultants and labor relations firms
industries.note: The bill's findings put this industry at roughly $340 million a year in fees from companies trying to sway workers against unions. Their fees would become non-deductible for clients and the consultants would have to file reports naming clients, dates, and amounts — shrinking demand and ending the anonymity of the work.

industries.industry: Anti-union employers (retail, logistics, hospitality, and other large workforces)
industries.note: Companies that run captive-audience meetings, surveillance, and consultant campaigns against organizing would lose the tax write-off and face reporting penalties that scale with headcount. Their interest in deducting these costs runs directly against workers' organizing rights, which is exactly the conduct the bill targets.

industries.industry: Labor unions and worker organizing groups
industries.note: Unions gain a fairer organizing environment: employer campaigns get more expensive, less subsidized, and publicly traceable, which tends to improve union win rates in representation elections. The bill also exempts amounts paid by labor organizations from its penalties.

industries.industry: All employers with HR and training programs
industries.note: Even employers that do not oppose unions bear compliance costs, because any meeting or training at which labor organizations are discussed becomes non-deductible and reportable. The bill's exceptions for bargaining, grievance procedures, and required postings limit but do not eliminate this burden.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican support and a Republican majority controlling the Ways and Means Committee's calendar, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or floor vote in the 119th Congress. The most probable path is that it sits in committee until the session ends in January 2027 and is reintroduced if Democrats take the majority; its large sponsor list mainly preserves it as a stated priority rather than a live measure.
